name: Treaty with the Shoshoni-Northwestern Bands, 1863 (Treaty of Box Elder)
area: Northern Utah and southern Idaho, the country of the Northwestern Shoshone; Article 4 bounds Pokatello's country by the Raft River on the west and the Portneuf Mountains on the east. It ceded no land, so Royce has no cession for it.
presentDayTribes: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation
nations: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation (Newe)
promises: Article 1: friendly relations re-established and a firm and perpetual peace.
Article 2: the bands gave their full assent to the Fort Bridger treaty of July 2, 1863 with the Shoshone Nation and adopted its provisions as part of this agreement.
Article 3: the United States would increase the Shoshone Nation's annuity by $5,000, paid as under the Fort Bridger treaty; the bands acknowledged receiving $2,000 in provisions and goods at signing.
Article 5: nothing in the treaty admitted any greater Indian title to the land than existed under Mexican law.
compensation: No land payment; the treaty took no land. The Supreme Court refused the bands' claim under it in 1945.
today: The treaty was signed six months after the Bear River Massacre of January 29, 1863, in which, the Northwestern Band says, U.S. Army volunteers under Colonel Patrick E. Connor killed some 350 Northwestern Shoshone; Connor signed this treaty for the United States.

nationVoice.nation: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
nationVoice.summary: Describes Box Elder as a peace treaty with no land cession in which the band allowed safe passage and the government agreed to provide goods and services, signed after the Bear River Massacre.

openQuestions: In Northwestern Bands of Shoshone Indians v. United States, 324 U.S. 335 (1945), the Supreme Court held that the treaty did not recognise Indian title to the lands, so the bands' land claim did not arise under it; Justice Jackson's concurrence nonetheless spoke of a moral obligation to the Shoshone. That ruling is evidence against a breach of this treaty's land terms, not for one.
Whether the $5,000 annuity increase was paid was not researched.
The bands' later Indian Claims Commission claim for aboriginal lands (with the Shoshone-Bannock, Docket 326 series) was not traced.
The Bear River Massacre preceded this treaty and is not counted as a breach of it.

Audit 2026-11-08: area no longer names the Bear River as a boundary (Article 4 names only the Raft River and the Portneuf Mountains, for Pokatello's country); Article 2 no longer attributes the Fort Bridger treaty's road and passage terms to this text, which only adopts that treaty; Article 3 wording matched to the text (the $2,000 was acknowledged as received).

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for Shoshone and Northwestern Bands (Court of Claims index) and 'Shoshone Box Elder', 'Northwestern Shoshone 1863' (ICC); nothing new. The Docket 326 findings of October 16, 1962 (OSU id 755) describe this treaty and the bands' ties to the Fort Bridger treaty but make no finding that its terms were broken; 95, 100 and 103 Ct. Cl. lead to the 1945 Supreme Court ruling already recorded.
